item.title: Climate warming can slow how tree roots feed soil microbes
item.description: A plant's roots do much of their work out of sight, pulling in water and nutrients and holding the plant in place. That makes it hard to see how plants respond when conditions underground change, and how a warming climate affects them. New Dartmouth-led studies look at the strategies plants use below the surface to adapt and survive. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Supercooled clouds over the highest mountains respond differently to climate change
item.description: Most studies of how clouds are responding to climate change focus on clouds over the oceans, rather than over mountains. Those that do focus on mountain clouds tend to explore cloud microphysics rather than long-term trends in cloud phase. But understanding cloud behavior over regions such as the Tibetan Plateau, which supplies water to hundreds of millions of people, is critical—especially as diminishing snowpack and altered precipitation patterns threaten this critical water source. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: La ciudad subterránea de Roma: ¿un refugio ante el calor extremo?
item.description: Desde Roma, en esta emisión de Enlace, nos adentramos bajo tierra para descubrir una posible respuesta de la capital italiana a la emergencia climática. Un equipo de científicos estudia cómo aprovechar la extensa red de espacios subterráneos de la ciudad -con más de 5.000 catacumbas, cuevas y antiguas canteras censadas- para ofrecer resguardo frente a las temperaturas extremas. Acompañamos a geólogos, urbanistas y vecinos en situación de vulnerabilidad para explorar el potencial de estos espacios y analizar los desafíos técnicos y urbanísticos que plantea su uso, en una ciudad cada vez más… Fuente: France 24 - Español.

item.title: Forecasting 'tipping points' with AI climate simulation
item.description: The writer Malcolm Gladwell popularized the term "tipping points" to refer to the moment when a trend or social behavior crosses a threshold and rapidly spreads everywhere. In physics, tipping points occur when systems—say, Earth's climate—reach an unstable point and topple over into a sea of change that is sometimes irreversible. Examples include global warming or the melting of polar ice caps. Fuente: Phys.org.
